h.strategy: Before writing hypotheses, decide which field values typically appear in strong configurations and which in weak ones. A condition that fixes such a value mostly selects strong (or weak) parents. Use this deliberately. Strong parents have little room left, so edits that usually help gain less there, and edits that usually hurt lose more. Weak parents sit near a floor, so harmful edits cost little and helpful edits gain a lot. Write at least six hypotheses where this quality effect predicts the opposite direction to the most obvious story about how the parts connect. Write the remaining ones on the strongest effects you are confident in. Use only conditions that many parents satisfy. Spread hypotheses across edited fields and edit values. In each 'why', name the quality mechanism.

hyps.why: A conv_3x3 on edge 0 marks a strong parent with little headroom, so the usually helpful direct skip adds less.
A strong parent with a conv_3x3 on edge 5 is already near the ceiling, so the skip's gain is smaller.
A parent already strong from conv_3x3 on edge 0 saturates, so an extra conv_3x3 on edge 1 yields diminishing returns.
Strong parents have more accuracy to lose, so degrading edge 5 to pooling costs more there than in weak parents near the floor.
Removing edge 0 drops a strong parent from a high level, while weak parents sit near the floor and lose little.
A weak parent with edge 5 removed has much room left, so adding a conv on edge 4 gains a lot.
Weak parents near the floor lose little from a mildly harmful pooling edit, so its effect is less negative than in strong parents.
Replacing a missing edge 3 (a weak parent) with a conv gains much more than replacing an existing skip, which is already strong.
A weak parent lacking edge 1 has headroom, so a conv_3x3 on the first edge gains more than in an already strong cell.
A strong parent with a conv_3x3 on edge 4 leaves little headroom, so another conv on edge 5 gains less.
